```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE,
  message = FALSE,
  warning = TRUE,
  fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 3.6,
  fig.align = "center",
  out.width = "90%",
  fig.pos = "H",
  out.extra = ""
)

library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)

# Import the data
cases.2 <- read_tsv("cases-2.tsv", show_col_types = FALSE)
population.2 <- read_tsv("population-2.tsv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Define the order of the age groups
age_order <- c(
  "0-4", "5-9", "10-14", "15-19", "20-24", "25-29",
  "30-34", "35-39", "40-44", "45-49", "50-54", "55-59",
  "60-64", "65-69", "70-74", "75-79", "80-84", "85-89"
)

# Define sex categories and colours
sexes <- c("Female", "Male")
cols <- c(Female = "#B34D70", Male = "#227C9D")
```

# Introduction

This assignment analyses colon cancer cases in Sweden from 1970
to 2022 by calendar year, age group and sex. The supplied data
cover people aged 0–89 years.

# Question 1: Cases by age group and sex

The merged dataset, called `cases`, contains five-year age groups,
sex, calendar year, the number of incident cases (`n`) and the
population size (`n_pop`), with each row representing an age-year-sex
combination.

We sum the cases across calendar years within each age group
and sex to compare their overall distributions over the study period.

```{r q1-aggregate, echo=TRUE}
cases <- left_join(cases.2, population.2,
                   by = c("agegroup", "sex", "year"))
cases$agegroup <- factor(cases$agegroup, levels = age_order)
by_age <- aggregate(n ~ agegroup + sex, cases, sum)
```

```{r q1-prepare, include=FALSE}
by_age$agegroup <- factor(by_age$agegroup, levels = age_order)
```

```{r q1-plot, fig.height=3, fig.cap="Colon cancer cases pooled over 1970–2022, by age group and sex."}
ggplot(by_age, aes(x = agegroup, y = n, fill = sex)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ sex) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cols) +
  labs(
    title = "Number of cases by age group and sex",
    x = "Age group",
    y = "Cases"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    legend.position = "none"
  )
```

Case counts generally increase with age,
reaching a peak at ages 75–79 for both sexes before decreasing
in the oldest age groups. This decrease does not necessarily
indicate a lower incidence rate, because population sizes
differ across age groups.

# Question 2: Annual cases by sex

We sum the cases across age groups, retaining one total
for each calendar year and sex.

```{r q2-aggregate, echo=TRUE}
annual_cases <- aggregate(n ~ year + sex, cases, sum)
```

```{r q2-plot, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Annual colon cancer cases, ages 0–89, separately by sex."}
old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

for (s in sexes) {
  a <- annual_cases[annual_cases$sex == s, ]
  a <- a[order(a$year), ]

  plot(
    a$year, a$n,
    type = "l",
    col = cols[s],
    main = s,
    xlab = "Year",
    ylab = "Annual cases",
    ylim = range(annual_cases$n)
  )
}

par(old_par)
```

The figure shows an increase in recorded
cases for both sexes. Female counts rise from 1,196 in 1970
to 2,713 in 2022, while male counts rise from 1,093 to 2,713 over the same period.
However, these counts do not distinguish between changes in population
size, age composition and incidence.

# Question 3: Population size by age, year and sex

The second dataset, called `population.2`, is structured similarly
to the cases dataset, providing a column named `n_pop` for population size.

We plot population trajectories covering all calendar years, comparing females
and males using coloured lines. Population labels are displayed
in thousands.

```{r q3-prepare, echo=TRUE}
population_plot <- population.2 %>%
  mutate(agegroup = factor(agegroup, levels = age_order))
```

```{r q3-plot, fig.cap="Population size over all years from 1970 to 2022.", fig.height=6.2, fig.width=7, out.width="90%"}
ggplot(
  population_plot,
  aes(x = year, y = n_pop, colour = sex)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ agegroup, ncol = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = cols) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(1970, 1990, 2010, 2022)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = function(x) x / 1000
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Population size over time by age group and sex",
    x = "Calendar year",
    y = "Population (thousands)",
    colour = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )
```

Population size changes over time, and these
changes differ across age groups. The proportion of individuals aged 65–89 increases
from approximately 15.3% to 21.9% among females and from 12.3%
to 19.0% among males. Therefore, the population is ageing for both sexes. This matters because age composition
influences the crude incidence rate.

# Question 4: Merging and summarising 

```{r q4-merge, echo=TRUE}
cases <- left_join(cases.2, population.2
                , by = c("agegroup", "sex", "year"))
head(cases)
summarize <- cases %>%
  group_by(year, sex) %>%
  summarise(
    n = sum(n, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_pop = sum(n_pop, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

The `cases` data frame retains the population at risk in each year for each age group and sex, whereas `summarize` aggregates total cases and total population size. In the population file, the age groups and calendar years are the same; all the year-sex-age combinations match perfectly.

# Question 5: Incidence rates

```{r q5-rate, echo=TRUE}
cases$rate <- cases$n / cases$n_pop
summarize$rate <- summarize$n / summarize$n_pop
cases$rate100k <- 100000 * cases$rate
summarize$rate100k <- 100000 * summarize$rate
```

An incidence rate measures the frequency of development of a disease over a population. In this case it has been calculated for both datasets and it has been multiplied by 100,000 so that the result is easier to compare, representing the number of cases per 100,000 individuals. While useful for observing the impact of a disease over a population, crude rates are affected by age structure and require a standardization to avoid any confounders.

# Question 6: Trends in incidence rates

```{r q6-plot, echo=TRUE, fig.cap="Crude incidence rate of colon cancer per 100,000 person-years by calendar year, with a smoothing spline (black line), separately by sex."}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
for (s in sexes) {
  a <- summarize[summarize$sex == s, ]; a <- a[order(a$year), ]
  plot(a$year, a$rate100k, type = 'o', pch = 16, cex = 0.4,
       col = cols[s], main = s, ylim = range(summarize$rate100k),
       xlab = 'Year', ylab = 'Rate per 100,000 person-years')
  sm <- smooth.spline(x = a$year, y = a$rate100k,
                      cv = FALSE, all.knots = TRUE)
  year_grid <- seq(min(a$year), max(a$year), length.out = 300)
  fitted_curve <- predict(sm, x = year_grid)
  lines(fitted_curve$x, fitted_curve$y, lwd = 2)
  legend('topleft', c('Observed rate', 'Smoothing spline'),
         col = c(cols[s], 'black'), lty = c(1, 1),
         pch = c(16, NA), bty = 'n', cex = 0.7)
}
```

Crude incidence rates per 100,000 person-years have been plotted (Figure 4) for both males and females alongside cubic smoothing splines. From the graphs, an almost constant growth is present for both sexes, with larger year-to-year fluctuations in females. Although the crude values of the incidence rates are somewhat higher for women, the gap tends to narrow as time passes, reaching similar levels in 2022. However, as we stated in Question 5, age is a confounder for the crude incidence rate, therefore part of the upward trend reflects people ageing.

# Question 7: Poisson regression for the total number of cases

```{r q7-data}
# Total cases and population per calendar year and sex (summed over age groups)
# (`cases` = merged age-specific data from Question 4)
total_data <- cases %>%
  group_by(year, sex) %>%
  summarise(n = sum(n), n_pop = sum(n_pop), .groups = "drop")

total_data$rate100k <- 1e5 * total_data$n / total_data$n_pop              # observed crude rate
total_data$year0 <- total_data$year - 1970                                # year centred at 1970
total_data$sex   <- factor(total_data$sex, levels = c("Male", "Female"))  # Male = reference
```

Let $Y_{ts}$ be the number of cases in year $t$ and sex $s$, and $P_{ts}$ the population size. The model is

$$Y_{ts} \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu_{ts}), \qquad
\log(\mu_{ts}) = \log(P_{ts}) + \beta_0 + \beta_1(\text{year}_t - 1970) + \beta_2\,\text{Female}_s .$$

```{r q7-model, echo=TRUE}
# Final model: Poisson, offset = log(population), linear year + sex
m_total <- glm(n ~ year0 + sex + offset(log(n_pop)),
               family = poisson(link = "log"), data = total_data)

# Rate ratios with 95% Wald confidence intervals 
# (intercept row dropped: it is the 1970 male rate)
est <- coef(m_total); se <- sqrt(diag(vcov(m_total)))
rr_total <- exp(cbind(RR = est, lower = est - 1.96 * se, upper = est + 1.96 * se))[-1, ]
round(rr_total, 4)
```

```{r q7-check, echo=TRUE}
# Support for the modelling choices: spline for year, and year-by-sex interaction
library(splines)
m_spline <- update(m_total, . ~ ns(year0, df = 3) + sex + offset(log(n_pop)))
m_int    <- update(m_total, . ~ year0 * sex + offset(log(n_pop)))

a_spline <- anova(m_total, m_spline, test = "Chisq")   
# likelihood-ratio test: linear vs spline
a_int    <- anova(m_total, m_int,    test = "Chisq")   
# likelihood-ratio test: no interaction vs interaction
a_spline; a_int
AIC(m_total, m_spline, m_int)

# Quantities used in the text
p_spline <- a_spline$`Pr(>Chi)`[2]
p_int    <- a_int$`Pr(>Chi)`[2]
max_diff_spline <- 100 * max(abs(fitted(m_spline) / fitted(m_total) - 1))  
# spline vs linear fit, %
rr_year_male   <- exp(coef(m_int)["year0"])
rr_year_female <- exp(coef(m_int)["year0"] + coef(m_int)["year0:sexFemale"])
disp_pois <- sum(residuals(m_total, type = "pearson")^2) / df.residual(m_total)  
# Pearson chi2 / df
```

**Motivation.** We model rates instead of counts, since the number of cases depends on the size of the population. This is done by including $\log(\text{population})$ as an offset (its coefficient is fixed to 1), so the exponentiated coefficients are rate ratios. Calendar year is included as a continuous, linear term on the log scale. This gives a smooth curve and one easily interpreted rate ratio per year, which fits the aim of smoothing the random variation between years. The likelihood-ratio test (p = `r format.pval(p_spline, digits = 2)`) and the AIC both favour a more flexible spline, so the trend is not perfectly log-linear. We still keep the linear term as a deliberate simplification, because the spline changes the fitted rates by at most `r round(max_diff_spline, 1)`%, which is small compared with the overall increase. Part of the non-linearity is probably also due to the changing age structure, which is handled in Questions 10-13. The spline fit is shown in Figure 6 as a sensitivity analysis.

Sex is included as a binary factor (male as reference) with a main effect only, which gives one constant female/male rate ratio. A year-by-sex interaction is statistically supported (p = `r format.pval(p_int, digits = 2)`), but the yearly rate ratios are similar for males (`r round(rr_year_male, 4)`) and females (`r round(rr_year_female, 4)`). We therefore keep the simpler model, and state the limitation in Question 8.

**Interpretation.** The estimated rate ratio per calendar year is `r round(rr_total["year0", "RR"], 4)` (95% CI `r round(rr_total["year0", "lower"], 4)`-`r round(rr_total["year0", "upper"], 4)`), i.e. the incidence rate increases by about `r round(100 * (rr_total["year0", "RR"] - 1), 1)`% per year. The rate among females is `r round(rr_total["sexFemale", "RR"], 3)` times the rate among males (95% CI `r round(rr_total["sexFemale", "lower"], 3)`-`r round(rr_total["sexFemale", "upper"], 3)`), after taking calendar year into account.

# Question 8: Estimated incidence rates in 1970 and 2020

```{r q8-pred, echo=TRUE}
# Predicted rates per 100,000 person-years (population set to 100,000, 
# so exp(fit) is the rate)
newdata_q8 <- expand.grid(year = c(1970, 2020),
                          sex = factor(c("Male", "Female"), levels = c("Male", "Female")),
                          n_pop = 1e5)
newdata_q8$year0 <- newdata_q8$year - 1970

pred_q8 <- predict(m_total, newdata = newdata_q8, type = "link", se.fit = TRUE)
newdata_q8$rate  <- exp(pred_q8$fit)
newdata_q8$lower <- exp(pred_q8$fit - 1.96 * pred_q8$se.fit)
newdata_q8$upper <- exp(pred_q8$fit + 1.96 * pred_q8$se.fit)

res_q8 <- newdata_q8[order(newdata_q8$year, newdata_q8$sex), 
                     c("year", "sex", "rate", "lower", "upper")]
knitr::kable(res_q8, digits = 1, row.names = FALSE, position = "H",
             col.names = 
               c("Year", "Sex", "Rate per 100,000", "Lower 95% CI", "Upper 95% CI"),
             caption = 
               "Estimated incidence rate per 100,000 person-years in 1970 and 2020, by sex.")

# Values used in the text
r <- setNames(res_q8$rate, paste(res_q8$sex, res_q8$year, sep = "_"))
b <- unname(coef(m_total))   # (Intercept), year0, sexFemale
```

**Interpretation.** According to the model (Table 1), the incidence rate in 1970 was `r round(r["Male_1970"], 1)` per 100,000 person-years among males and `r round(r["Female_1970"], 1)` among females. In 2020 the estimated rates were `r round(r["Male_2020"], 1)` among males and `r round(r["Female_2020"], 1)` among females. The rate ratio per calendar year is `r round(exp(b[2]), 4)`, i.e. an increase of about `r round(100 * (exp(b[2]) - 1), 1)`% per year and `r round(100 * (exp(50 * b[2]) - 1), 0)`% between 1970 and 2020. The rate for females is `r round(exp(b[3]), 3)` times the rate for males.

**Assumptions.** We have assumed that the log incidence rate changes linearly with calendar year, so that the rate changes by the same percentage every year. The tests in Question 7 show that this is only an approximation. We have also assumed that the yearly change is the same for males and females, and that the female/male rate ratio is the same in every year. The absolute difference between the sexes can still change over time, since it is constant only on the multiplicative scale, and the interaction in Question 7 suggests that the yearly increase is slightly smaller among females. Finally, we have assumed that the number of cases is Poisson distributed and independent across years and sexes, that the population on July 1st approximates the person-years at risk, and that the crude rates over ages 0-89 are not adjusted for age (done in Question 10). The Pearson $\chi^2$/df is `r round(disp_pois, 2)`, which is above 1, so there is more variation than a Poisson model allows and the confidence intervals are probably somewhat too narrow; the point estimates are not affected.

# Question 9: Estimated incidence rates over calendar year by sex

```{r q9-data}
# Model-based rates for every calendar year, per 100,000 person-years
grid_q9 <- expand.grid(year = 1970:2022,
                       sex = factor(c("Male", "Female"), levels = c("Male", "Female")),
                       n_pop = 1e5)
grid_q9$year0 <- grid_q9$year - 1970

pred_q9 <- predict(m_total, newdata = grid_q9, type = "link", se.fit = TRUE)
grid_q9$rate  <- exp(pred_q9$fit)
grid_q9$lower <- exp(pred_q9$fit - 1.96 * pred_q9$se.fit)
grid_q9$upper <- exp(pred_q9$fit + 1.96 * pred_q9$se.fit)
grid_q9$rate_spline <- exp(predict(m_spline, newdata = grid_q9, type = "link"))  # sensitivity
```

```{r q9-plot, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Model-based incidence rates (solid, with 95% CI) and observed crude rates (points) by calendar year and sex. Dashed lines are loess smoothers of the observed rates.", echo=TRUE}
ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(data = grid_q9, aes(year, ymin = lower, ymax = upper, fill = sex), 
              alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(data = grid_q9, aes(year, rate, colour = sex), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = total_data, aes(year, rate100k, colour = sex), size = 1, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(data = total_data, aes(year, rate100k, colour = sex), method = "loess",
              formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = cols) + scale_fill_manual(values = cols) +
  labs(title = "Estimated incidence rate of colon cancer by calendar year",
       x = "Calendar year", y = "Rate per 100,000 person-years", colour = "Sex", 
       fill = "Sex") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r q9-plot2, echo=TRUE, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Sensitivity analysis (log scale): linear model (solid), spline model (dotted), loess of observed rates (dashed)."}
ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = total_data, aes(year, rate100k, colour = sex), size = 1, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(data = grid_q9, aes(year, rate, colour = sex), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_line(data = grid_q9, aes(year, rate_spline, colour = sex), linetype = "dotted", 
            linewidth = 1) +
  geom_smooth(data = total_data, aes(year, rate100k, colour = sex), method = "loess",
              formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_y_log10() + scale_colour_manual(values = cols) +
  labs(title = "Estimated incidence rate (log scale)", x = "Calendar year",
       y = "Rate per 100,000 person-years (log scale)", colour = "Sex") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r q9-ratio, echo=TRUE}
# Observed / fitted rate by period (>1 means the model underestimates the observed rate)
total_data$ratio  <- total_data$rate100k / (1e5 * fitted(m_total) / total_data$n_pop)
total_data$period <- cut(total_data$year, c(1969, 1980, 1990, 2000, 2010, 2022),
                         labels = c("1970-80", "1981-90", "1991-2000", "2001-10", "2011-22"))
ratio_tab <- round(tapply(total_data$ratio, list(total_data$period, total_data$sex), 
                          mean), 3)
knitr::kable(ratio_tab, position = "H", 
             caption = "Mean observed / fitted rate by period and sex.")
```

**Interpretation.** The estimated incidence rate of colon cancer increases steadily in both sexes (Figure 5), from about `r round(r["Male_1970"], 0)`-`r round(r["Female_1970"], 0)` per 100,000 person-years in 1970 to about `r round(r["Male_2020"], 0)`-`r round(r["Female_2020"], 0)` in 2020, and it is somewhat higher among females throughout (by `r round(100 * (exp(b[3]) - 1), 1)`% in the model). The model curves remove the random year-to-year variation seen in the observed rates, and the loess smoothers follow the model lines fairly closely, so a log-linear trend is a reasonable summary.

There are, however, systematic departures (see Table 2). Observed female rates are above the model line in 1981-90 (`r ratio_tab["1981-90", "Female"]` times the fitted rate) and below it in 2001-10 and 2011-22 (`r ratio_tab["2001-10", "Female"]` and `r ratio_tab["2011-22", "Female"]`), while male rates are below it in the 1970s (`r ratio_tab["1970-80", "Male"]`) and above it in 2011-22 (`r ratio_tab["2011-22", "Male"]`). The observed rates of the two sexes therefore move closer over time, whereas the model keeps a constant ratio, which agrees with the interaction in Question 7. The spline model follows the loess curves a little better (Figure 6) but differs little from the linear model. Finally, the rates are crude (not age-adjusted), so part of the increase and of the departures from a straight line may be due to the ageing of the population (Figure 3), which is addressed in Questions 10-13.

# Question 10: Adjusted model for age

As shown in previous tasks, colon cancer occurs predominantly in older age groups, and the Swedish population aged substantially between 1970 and 2022. To separate true temporal changes in incidence from demographic shifts in age structure, we fit a Poisson regression model to the age-specific dataset (`cases`). Let $Y_{ats}$ be the number of cases in age group $a$, calendar year $t$, and sex $s$, and $P_{ats}$ the corresponding population size:
$$Y_{ats} \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu_{ats}),$$
$$\log(\mu_{ats}) = \log(P_{ats}) + \beta_0 + \alpha_a + f(\text{year}_t - 1970) + \beta_{\text{sex}}\text{Female}_s.$$

First, we define the age groups in chronological order, centre calendar year at 1970 (`year0`), and set `Male` as the reference category. We create different Poisson models and compare them in order to see which one fits the data better:

```{r q10-fit, echo=TRUE}
library(splines)

cases$agegroup <- factor(cases$agegroup, levels = age_order)
cases$sex      <- factor(cases$sex, levels = c("Male", "Female"))
cases$year0    <- cases$year - 1970

# Poisson models: linear year vs. natural cubic spline (df = 4)
m10_lin <- glm(
  n ~ agegroup + year0 + sex + offset(log(n_pop)),
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  data = cases
)

m10_spline <- glm(
  n ~ agegroup + ns(year0, df = 4) + sex + offset(log(n_pop)),
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  data = cases
)

# Likelihood-ratio test and AIC: linear vs. spline
anova(m10_lin, m10_spline, test = "Chisq")
AIC(m10_lin, m10_spline)
```

**Motivation and interpretation.**

* **Distribution and offset:** Because case counts depend on population size, $\log(\text{n\_pop})$ is included as an offset (coefficient fixed to $1$) so that the model estimates incidence rates.

* **Age group (`agegroup`):** Modelled as a categorical factor with 18 five-year levels (`0-4` as reference). Incidence rises steeply with age, and the population has aged over the study period (Figure 3), so age is the main confounder of the trend over calendar years. A categorical factor lets each age group have its own effect without assuming a linear or exponential shape across age.

* **Calendar year:** Because the age structure changes over time, we check whether a non-linear trend is still needed after adjusting for age. A natural cubic spline with four degrees of freedom replaces the linear term. The likelihood-ratio test gives χ²(3) = 48.75, p = 1.5e-10, and the AIC is 12619.57 for the linear model and 12576.82 for the spline, so the spline is kept. Four degrees of freedom is a moderate level of flexibility.

* **Sex (`sex`):** Modelled as a binary factor (`Male` as reference) so the model estimates one female-to-male rate ratio adjusted for age and calendar year.

# Question 11: Incidence rate in 1970 and 2020 in ages 52, 72 and 87 (males and females)

To obtain the model-based incidence rates from `m10_spline`, we create a prediction grid containing the 12 combinations of exact age (`52`, `72`, `87`), calendar year (`1970`, `2020`), and sex (`Male`, `Female`). Each exact age is mapped to its corresponding five-year age group (`50-54`, `70-74`, and `85-89`), calendar year is centred at 1970 (`year0`), and `n_pop` is set to `100,000` so that `predict(..., type = "response")` directly returns incidence rates per 100,000 person-years.

```{r q11-predict, echo=TRUE}
pred_grid <- expand.grid(
  age   = c(52, 72, 87),
  year  = c(1970, 2020),
  sex   = factor(c("Male", "Female"), levels = levels(cases$sex)),
  n_pop = 100000
)

# Map each exact age (52, 72, 87) to its corresponding 5-year age group
pred_grid$agegroup <- factor(
  ifelse(pred_grid$age == 52, "50-54",
         ifelse(pred_grid$age == 72, "70-74", "85-89")),
  levels = age_order
)
pred_grid$year0 <- pred_grid$year - 1970

# Predicted incidence rates per 100,000 person-years
pred_grid$rate100k <- predict(m10_spline, newdata = pred_grid, type = "response")

res_q11 <- pred_grid[order(pred_grid$year, pred_grid$sex, pred_grid$age),
                     c("year", "sex", "age", "agegroup", "rate100k")]

knitr::kable(
  res_q11,
  digits = 1,
  row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Year", "Sex", "Age", "Age group", "Rate per 100,000"),
  caption = "Estimated colon cancer incidence rates per 100,000 person-years in 1970 and 2020 at ages 52, 72 and 87."
)
```

**Interpretation.** The exact ages 52, 72 and 87 are the midpoints of the age groups 50–54, 70–74 and 85–89, so the estimated rate of each group is used at these ages. Rates rise steeply with age: at age 87 the rate is about 10.5 times the rate at age 52 in both years. Between 1970 and 2020 the rate increases by 31% at every age and in both sexes (rate ratio 1.31). This is much smaller than the 73% increase in Question 8, which did not adjust for age, so population ageing explains a large part of the crude increase (see Question 12). At every age the female rate is 14% lower than the male rate (rate ratio 0.856).

**Assumptions.**

1. **Change over calendar years:** The log rate follows the same spline in calendar year at all ages and in both sexes, since there is no year-by-age interaction. The 31% increase is therefore the same for every age and sex.

2. **Change across age:** Age is a step function over 5-year groups, so all single ages within a group share the group's rate.

3. **Males and females:** The female-to-male rate ratio (0.856) is the same at every age and in every year. This is a simplification: the year-by-sex interaction in Question 7 was significant (p = 3.6e-07), so the yearly increase may be slightly smaller among females. On the absolute scale the sex gap grows with age: in 2020 it is 41.1 per 100,000 at age 87 and 3.9 at age 52.

4. **Different ages within different years:** Age and calendar year are additive on the log scale, so the ratio between ages 87 and 52 (about 10.5) is the same in 1970 and 2020.

# Question 12: Direct age-standardised incidence rates

To compare colon cancer incidence across calendar years without distortion from population ageing, we compute **direct age-standardised incidence rates** for each calendar year and sex using the **2022 sex-specific Swedish age distribution** as the standard population weights. We then compare these standardised rates with the unadjusted model-based rates from Question 9 (which did not include age).

```{r q12-standardised, echo=TRUE}
# 1. Standard population: age distribution of each sex in 2022
std_2022 <- cases %>%
  filter(year == 2022) %>%
  group_by(sex) %>%
  mutate(weight = n_pop / sum(n_pop)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(agegroup, sex, weight)

# 2. Direct age-standardised rates per 100,000 person-years, by year and sex
dsr_data <- cases %>%
  mutate(rate100k = 100000 * (n / n_pop)) %>%
  left_join(std_2022, by = c("agegroup", "sex")) %>%
  group_by(year, sex) %>%
  summarise(
    dsr100k = sum(rate100k * weight),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# 3. Unadjusted rates from the Poisson model of Question 7 (same as Question 9)
compare_q12 <- total_data %>%
  mutate(unadj_model100k = 100000 * fitted(m_total) / n_pop) %>%
  left_join(dsr_data, by = c("year", "sex"))

# Values used in the text
d     <- setNames(dsr_data$dsr100k, paste(dsr_data$sex, dsr_data$year, sep = "_"))
rq    <- setNames(grid_q9$rate,     paste(grid_q9$sex, grid_q9$year, sep = "_"))
pm_d  <- round(100 * (d["Male_2022"]   / d["Male_1970"]   - 1), 1)
pf_d  <- round(100 * (d["Female_2022"] / d["Female_1970"] - 1), 1)
pm_rq <- round(100 * (rq["Male_2022"]   / rq["Male_1970"]   - 1), 1)
pf_rq <- round(100 * (rq["Female_2022"] / rq["Female_1970"] - 1), 1)
share_m <- round(100 * (1 - pm_d / pm_rq))
share_f <- round(100 * (1 - pf_d / pf_rq))
```


```{r q12-plot, fig.height=3.6, fig.cap="Direct age-standardised colon cancer incidence rates (2022 sex-specific standard population) compared with the unadjusted model from Question 9, by calendar year and sex."}
cols_q12 <- c("Female" = "#B34D70", "Male" = "#227C9D")

ggplot(compare_q12, aes(x = year, colour = sex)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = dsr100k), size = 1.1, alpha = 0.55) +
  geom_smooth(
    aes(y = dsr100k, linetype = "Age-standardised (2022 std)"),
    method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.9
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = unadj_model100k, linetype = "Unadjusted model (Q9)"),
    linewidth = 0.9
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = cols_q12) +
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = c(
      "Age-standardised (2022 std)" = "solid",
      "Unadjusted model (Q9)"       = "dashed"
    )
  ) +
  guides(
    linetype = guide_legend(override.aes = list(colour = "black"))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Age-standardised vs. unadjusted colon cancer incidence rates",
    x = "Calendar year",
    y = "Rate per 100,000 person-years",
    colour = "Sex",
    linetype = "Rate type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.key.width = unit(1.35, "cm")
  )
```

**Comparison with Question 9 and conclusions.** Figure 7 compares the direct age-standardised rates with the unadjusted model from Question 9.

1. **Higher rates in 1970.** In 1970 the age-standardised rates are `r round(d["Male_1970"], 1)` for males and `r round(d["Female_1970"], 1)` for females per 100,000 person-years, above the unadjusted model rates (`r round(rq["Male_1970"], 1)` and `r round(rq["Female_1970"], 1)`). The 2022 population is older than the 1970 population (Figure 3), so the 2022 weights give more weight to the age groups with the highest incidence. The gap narrows over time, and in 2022 the two rates coincide by construction, since 2022 is the standard population.

2. **Population ageing explains a large part of the increase.** Between 1970 and 2022 the unadjusted model rate rises by `r pm_rq`% in both sexes, whereas the age-standardised rate rises by `r pm_d`% for males and `r pf_d`% for females. About `r share_m`% of the crude increase in males and `r share_f`% in females is therefore due to changes in the age structure. A real increase remains, since the age-standardised rates still rise over the period.

3. **Trends before and after 2000.** Female rates are nearly flat until the mid-1990s, from `r round(d["Female_1970"], 1)` in 1970 to `r round(d["Female_2000"], 1)` in 2000. Male rates rise more steadily over the same period, from `r round(d["Male_1970"], 1)` to `r round(d["Male_2000"], 1)`. After 2000 both sexes increase further, reaching `r round(d["Male_2022"], 1)` for males and `r round(d["Female_2022"], 1)` for females in 2022. This pattern is consistent with the non-linear trend in Question 10, although the loess curves are only a visual guide to the yearly values.

4. **Comparison between sexes.** The two curves are close and cross at some points, but they cannot be compared directly, because each sex is standardised to its own 2022 age distribution. Part of the female level reflects the older female population in 2022 (21.9% vs. 19.0% aged 65–89), which is built into the female standard. The sex comparison is made in Question 11, where the female rate is 14% lower than the male rate at every age.

**Overall.** The unadjusted rates overstate the increase in colon cancer incidence, because a large part of it reflects an ageing population. After standardisation the increase is smaller, but the age-standardised rates still rise, most visibly after 2000.

# Question 13: Model-based age-standardised incidence rates

This time we standardise the age-specific rates predicted by the age-adjusted model from Question 10 (`m10_spline`) instead of the observed ones, using the same 2022 sex-specific weights (`std_2022`) as in Question 12.

```{r q13-standardised, echo=TRUE}
# 1. Model-based age-specific rates per 100,000 for every age group, year and sex
#    (n_pop = 100,000, so the predicted count is the rate per 100,000)
grid_q13 <- expand.grid(agegroup = factor(age_order, levels = age_order),
                        year = 1970:2022,
                        sex = factor(c("Male", "Female"), levels = c("Male", "Female")),
                        n_pop = 1e5)
grid_q13$year0    <- grid_q13$year - 1970
grid_q13$rate100k <- predict(m10_spline, newdata = grid_q13, type = "response")

# 2. Weight with the 2022 sex-specific age distribution and sum over age groups,
#    then add the direct age-standardised rates from Question 12 for comparison
msr_data <- grid_q13 %>%
  left_join(std_2022, by = c("agegroup", "sex")) %>%
  group_by(year, sex) %>%
  summarise(msr100k = sum(rate100k * weight), .groups = "drop") %>%
  left_join(dsr_data, by = c("year", "sex"))

# Values used in the text
ms       <- setNames(msr_data$msr100k, paste(msr_data$sex, msr_data$year, sep = "_"))
p_ms     <- round(100 * (ms["Male_2022"] / ms["Male_1970"] - 1), 1)  # same for both sexes
fm_ms    <- round(ms["Female_2022"] / ms["Male_2022"], 3)            # female/male ratio
mean_dif <- round(mean(abs(100 * (msr_data$dsr100k / msr_data$msr100k - 1))), 1)  # mean |% diff|
```

```{r q13-plot, echo=TRUE, fig.height=3.4, fig.cap="Model-based age-standardised rates (lines) and direct age-standardised rates from Question 12 (points), 2022 sex-specific standard population."}
ggplot(msr_data, aes(x = year, colour = sex)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = dsr100k), size = 1.1, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(aes(y = msr100k), linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = cols) +
  labs(title = "Model-based vs. direct age-standardised incidence rates",
       x = "Calendar year", y = "Rate per 100,000 person-years", colour = "Sex") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The model-based standardised rates run through the middle of the direct standardised rates from Question 12 (Figure 8) and on average differ from them by `r mean_dif`%. They are smoother because they filter out the random fluctuations seen in the observed age-specific rates, which often rely on a limited number of cases.

However, the model-based rates also carry over the assumptions of the model. Because the model does not allow the trend over calendar years to differ between the sexes (there is no year-by-sex interaction), the rates increase by exactly `r p_ms`% between 1970 and 2022 for both males and females, and the female/male ratio stays the same every year (`r fm_ms`). This ratio is not the same as the age-specific ratio of 0.856, because each sex is standardised to its own age distribution and the female population is older. The direct rates show that the two sexes did not actually follow the same trend: they increase by `r pm_d`% for males but only `r pf_d`% for females. The model fits the male rates well, but underestimates the female rates in the 1970s (`r round(ms["Female_1970"], 1)` vs. `r round(d["Female_1970"], 1)` in 1970), a period when female rates were flat or slightly decreasing. To capture these sex-specific trends, the model would need a year-by-sex interaction, which the test in Question 7 supports.

# Question 14: Overall conclusions

```{r q14-values, echo=TRUE}
# Observed crude rates (Question 5) in 1970 and 2022, % increase by sex
cr   <- setNames(summarize$rate100k, paste(summarize$sex, summarize$year, sep = "_"))
p_cm <- round(100 * (cr["Male_2022"]   / cr["Male_1970"]   - 1))
p_cf <- round(100 * (cr["Female_2022"] / cr["Female_1970"] - 1))
```

Between 1970 and 2022 the number of colon cancer cases more than doubled in both sexes, and the crude incidence rate went up by `r p_cm`% among males and `r p_cf`% among females. Much of this increase comes from the population getting older. Once we adjust for age, the incidence still rises, but by less: `r pm_d`% among males and `r pf_d`% among females (2022 standard). The rise was also not even over time. Male rates went up slowly until about 2000 and faster after that, while female rates stayed roughly the same until about 2000 and only then started to rise. At the same age, women have about 14% lower incidence than men (Question 11), but because women live longer, the crude rates of the two sexes end up similar. These data cannot tell us why the age-adjusted incidence has increased; possible explanations include changes in risk factors such as diet, obesity and physical activity, and changes in how the disease is diagnosed.

Which rate to present depends on the question. Non-standardised (crude) rates show the actual burden of disease in the population, so they are the better choice for health-care planning. For example, a region estimating how many colonoscopies, operations and oncology resources it will need should use crude rates, because an older population really does produce more patients. Age-standardised rates take differences in age structure out of the picture, so they are the better choice for comparing the risk of disease between calendar years or between populations. Examples are checking whether the risk of colon cancer in Sweden has really changed since 1970, or comparing Sweden with a country that has a younger population. Age-standardised rates can only be compared with each other if they use the same standard population.
